scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

By fasting from dawn to sunset, individuals are forced to re-evaluate their relationship with food, water, and other daily comforts. This physical and mental challenge can lead to a greater appreciation for the simple things in life and a shift in focus towards more spiritual and meaningful aspects. The fact that everyone around you is also observing Ramadan creates a sense of community and shared experience, which can foster a deeper sense of empathy, compassion, and connection with others. This collective effort can lead to a greater emphasis on values like kindness, generosity, and selflessness. Moreover, the annual repetition of Ramadan can have a cumulative effect, allowing individuals to reflect on their personal growth, goals, and values over time. It's an opportunity to reassess priorities, let go of bad habits, and cultivate positive ones. This process of self-reflection and renewal can lead to a greater sense of purpose, gratitude, and contentment. Research has shown that experiences like Ramadan can have a lasting impact on individuals' values and behaviors, even after the month has ended. For example, studies have found that people who fast during Ramadan tend to be more charitable, volunteer more, and engage in more prosocial behaviors throughout the year. In terms of what people end up valuing most, I think Ramadan can lead to a greater emphasis on: 1. Spiritual growth and self-reflection 2. Community and social connections 3. Gratitude and appreciation for life's simple pleasures 4. Self-discipline and resilience 5. Empathy and compassion for others 6. Personal growth and self-improvement 7. Mindfulness and presence in daily life Of course, everyone's experience is unique, and the impact of Ramadan can vary from person to person. However, it's clear that this significant event can have a profound and lasting effect on individuals' values, priorities, and overall well-being.
